analysis.one_liner: Lets small businesses and self-employed people band together to buy health insurance exempt from some Obamacare rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was sent to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced, never received a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law rules allowing small employers, sole proprietors, and self-employed people to join "association health plans" — group insurance plans treated like large-employer coverage. It would also let short-term, limited-duration insurance plans last up to 12 months. These plans are exempt from some Affordable Care Act requirements, including coverage of preexisting conditions for short-term plans. The bill was a response to a March 2019 federal court decision that threw out a 2018 Labor Department rule expanding these plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Self-employed people, sole proprietors, and workers at small businesses who would gain access to cheaper group coverage by banding together across a state or metro area, with solo "working owners" treated as both employer and employee so they can join. Health insurers gain a new market of customers buying less-regulated plans.

how_it_helps.text: It lets groups of employers in the same trade or in the same state or metro area sponsor a group health plan as if they were a single large employer, pooling purchasing power to lower premiums.
It lets self-employed "working owners" count as both employer and employee, so people without any employees — freelancers, gig workers, sole proprietors — can join the plans.
The bill's findings cite average premium decreases of up to 29 percent for small businesses under association health plans.
It would restore legal authority for these plans after a federal district judge vacated the Labor Department's 2018 rule in March 2019, which the bill says threatened coverage for current enrollees.
The plans carry some protections: the bill bars conditioning membership or premiums on health factors and requires plans to follow federal nondiscrimination rules.

analysis.who_pays: People who stay in ACA-compliant coverage, especially those with preexisting conditions. Healthier people moving into cheaper association and short-term plans would leave the ACA risk pool with a sicker, more expensive population, pushing premiums up for everyone who remains. People buying the new plans would give up some ACA protections, and short-term plans can exclude coverage of preexisting conditions.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA enrollees, especially with preexisting conditions

drawbacks.text: Short-term, limited-duration plans are exempt from certain Affordable Care Act market requirements, such as coverage of individuals with preexisting conditions, so the plans this bill authorizes can offer skimpier coverage that fails people when they get sick.
Drawing healthier people out of ACA-compliant plans into cheaper, less-regulated ones raises costs for the people left in the ACA pool, who are disproportionately older and sicker.

The bill says participation in these plans cannot establish a joint-employer relationship under any federal or state law — including for franchisors, franchisees, and companies using independent contractors — shielding firms from being treated as jointly responsible for workers at franchise locations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a healthy freelancer or small business, cheaper pooled coverage is a real gain, and the bill does write in nondiscrimination rules so members cannot be turned away based on health status. But the cheapest plans would attract the healthiest people and leave ACA-compliant coverage more expensive for everyone else, and the short-term plans it authorizes can deny coverage of preexisting conditions. The bill also sneaks in a labor provision — a joint-employer shield for franchisors — unrelated to health coverage. On balance it trades a weaker insurance pool for cheaper options for some.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced in April 2019, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Enzi introduced the bill on April 11, 2019, with 25 Senate Republicans joining as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, which was its last action of record.
It gathered 30 Republican cosponsors in total and no Democratic cosponsors.
The committee never held a markup or sent the bill to the floor, and no vote ever took place in either chamber before the 116th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No law changed, so people in ACA-compliant plans kept the current risk pool and its protections, and insurers selling ACA marketplace coverage did not lose healthier customers to cheaper association plans. Self-employed people and small businesses did not get the cheaper coverage option the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA-compliant insurers and enrollees; status quo held

for.name: Mike Enzi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write the 2018 Labor Department association health plan rules into law after a court vacated them, and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 30 of 53 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never held a markup, reported it out, or sent it to the floor.

against.name: Federal district court (March 2019 ruling)
against.role: Court that vacated the 2018 Labor Department association health plan rule
against.what_they_did: Vacated the DOL final rule the bill sought to codify, which the bill's own findings cite as the reason for legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 30 cosponsors were Senate Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill died without either party bringing it to a vote.

industries.note: The bill creates a new market: insurers could sell association plans to pooled small businesses and self-employed people, and short-term plans could last up to 12 months. Insurers gain customers, but the plans are less regulated, and the healthiest buyers leaving ACA-compliant coverage would raise costs for everyone remaining in that pool.

industries.industry: Franchise chains and companies using independent contractors
industries.note: A provision in the bill states that sponsoring or facilitating these plans cannot create a joint-employer relationship under any federal or state law, covering franchisors, franchisees, and firms contracting with independent contractors. That shields companies from being treated as jointly responsible for workers' conditions at the same time it expands their benefits options.
